additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked negative symptoms seen in schizophrenia. Outside of the delusional beliefs, functioning is often relatively preserved and behavior may not appear obviously odd, which can delay recognition and treatment. The delusions tend to be non-bizarre or only moderately implausible, systematized, and fixed despite clear contradictory evidence, and are not better explained by mood disorders, substance use, or neurocognitive disorders. Onset is often in mid to late adulthood, and the course is typically chronic, with stressors, social isolation, or sensory and medical changes sometimes preceding or shaping the content of the delusional beliefs.

patient.personality: A meticulous, community-minded elder who prides himself on order, reliability, and being a respected organizer and storyteller in his neighborhood.
patient.stressor: About two years ago, Eliseo underwent a series of medical evaluations after a minor fall and some concerns about fluctuating blood pressure, which left him feeling scrutinized and frustrated when different providers gave him conflicting explanations. As someone who has always seen himself as the dependable supervisor who keeps systems running smoothly, these new health issues and occasional forgetfulness about medications felt like a loss of control and an affront to his self-image of competence. Over the following months, he became increasingly preoccupied with interpreting everyday events around his building, church, and the senior center in light of these health concerns, gradually reworking them into a fixed personal narrative that helped him make sense of his vulnerability but put him at odds with family and fellow volunteers. He finally came to psychiatric attention when his adult children and the senior center staff, worried that his increasingly insistent interpretations were straining relationships and complicating his care planning, persuaded his primary care doctor to refer him for a mental health evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m here because my family says I won’t let go of certain ideas, even when everyone tells me they’re wrong.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: Ever since all those doctors started poking and disagreeing about my blood pressure, I’ve been convinced the folks at the clinic and even some of the people at church are quietly coordinating things—like changing my appointment times, mixing up my pills, and passing little comments in the hallway—to see how much I can take and to push me out of my role as the one who keeps everything in order, and no matter how often my kids tell me it’s just mistakes or coincidences, I can see the pattern clear as day.
